activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Socks go on your feet before your shoes.
story:
Michael was shy at school. He liked to watch first. Today his class had a dress-up corner.

"Let's play getting ready," said Teacher Amy. "First we eat breakfast." Michael sniffed the play toast. He could smell the wooden toast, but it was just pretend. He laughed.

Next the dolls needed a nap. Michael patted a doll. He covered it with a small blanket. "Shh," he whispered. The doll slept and slept.

Then it was time to dress up. Michael wanted to wear the big red shoes. He pushed them onto his bare feet. His toes hurt. The shoes would not fit right. He sat down and tried again. Still wrong.

His friend Ben came over. "Watch me," said Ben. Ben put on his socks first. Then he pushed on his shoes. The shoes slid right on. "Socks first," said Ben.

Michael took the red shoes off. He wiggled his feet into the socks. Then he pushed on the shoes. They fit! He stood up and stomped around the rug.

"I did it!" said Michael. Ben clapped. Teacher Amy clapped too. Michael was not shy anymore. He stomped his feet all the way to the play kitchen.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food.
story:
Lincoln stood by the little bed. His new baby sister was in it. She was small and warm. She made a tiny sound.

Lincoln had a cracker in his hand. He wanted to share it. "Baby, want a bite?" he asked. He held it out to her. The baby turned her head away.

Mom came in. "Not a cracker, Lincoln," she said. "A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food." Lincoln looked at the bottle on the table. "Can I fetch it?" he asked. Mom smiled and gave him the bottle. It was warm in his hands.

Linlin watched Mom feed the baby. The baby drank and drank. Her tummy went round. She did not cry now. "She likes milk," Lincoln said. He patted her soft blanket. Then Mom went to wash dishes. Lincoln was not alone. He sat by the bed. He sang a little song, and the baby closed her eyes.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn.
story:
Charlie stood at the basketball court. The hoop was tall and far away. Charlie had a big red ball under her arm. Sam had five beanbags in a long row. "My turn, my turn," said Charlie. She picked up all the beanbags at once.

Sam's face went sad. Sam had no beanbags left. Coach Rosa knelt down beside them. "Taking turns," she said softly. One beanbag, then two beanbags. "You throw one. Then Sam has a turn." Charlie looked at the beanbags. One, two, three, four, five. She gave four to Sam. She kept just one.

Charlie threw her beanbag at the hoop. It went up, up, up. Then it came down and sat on the rim. It did not fall in. Sam threw one. Sam's beanbag went in. "Yay!" said Charlie. She clapped her hands. Then it was Charlie's turn again. This time her beanbag went in. The hoop made a little swish.

Then Coach Rosa rolled the big red ball to Charlie. Charlie held out both hands. Pat, pat, went the ball on her fingers. She caught it with two hands. "I caught it!" she said. Sam clapped too. Then it was Sam's turn to catch. Charlie rolled the ball, slow and gentle, all the way to Sam's two hands. "One throw for you," said Charlie. "One throw for me."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them.
story:
Lincoln ran to the school garden with his teacher, Ms. May. He had tiny carrot seeds in his hand. He made little holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in and patted them down. "Grow, grow, grow!" he said.

Every day Lincoln ran to the garden. One morning, little green leaves popped up. Lincoln clapped his hands. Then he saw green leaves in the wrong spot too. They grew between his carrots, close and messy. What a puzzle! "Are these baby carrots?" he asked himself. "No, they are too thick and all over the place."

Lincoln grabbed one thin stem and pulled hard. "Stop!" said Ms. May. "That one is a weed. Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them." Lincoln let go fast. "So the messy leaves are bad?" he asked. "Yes," said Ms. May. "Pull those out, and leave the carrot leaves alone."

Lincoln pulled the weeds one by one. The dirt looked neat again. His carrots had room to grow tall. Then, one sunny day, Lincoln saw something orange in the dirt. He pulled it up. It was a carrot! "Look at this!" he shouted. He held it up high, and his hands smelled like fresh dirt and salty sea air from the playground breeze. "Ms. May!" he called. "My seed made a carrot!"

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Health experts say to scrub your hands with soap for at least twenty seconds.
story:
Nora was at Grandma's house. Cookies were waiting on a plate. Nora wanted one, and they looked crunchy.

"Nora, first we wash," said Grandma. "You scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds." Nora put soap on her hands. She rinsed fast, right away. "That was too quick," said Grandma. "The soap did not have time to work."

Nora tried again. She made lots of bubbles. Grandma said, "We count slowly to twenty." They counted together. One, two, three. Nora kept scrubbing. The bubbles grew and grew. Twenty! Nora rinsed all the soap off. Her hands were clean.

Grandma handed her a cookie. "Crunchy," said Nora, taking a bite. Then she marched around the kitchen with her clean hands held up high. Grandma laughed and gave her the answer she wanted most: "Yes, you may have one more."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes loud sounds quieter.
story:
Emmett was helping Mama in the kitchen. He smelled something sweet. "Banana bread!" he said, sniffing with his nose. He tasted a tiny bit of batter on his finger. Sweet again. He touched the cold bowl with his hand. Brrr.

Then Mama plugged in the blender. It started. VROOM! So loud! Emmett jumped. He put his hands over his ears. The loud sound got small. It got quiet in his ears. He peeked at Mama. "My ears feel better," he said. "Does yours?" He gave her his one free hand. She laughed and put it on her ear.

The blender stopped. Emmett let go. He heard Mama again. He heard the birds outside too. "One nose, two ears," he counted. "Two eyes, one tongue, two hands." He looked at the wild steam. He saw Mama sweep the crumbs with her hand. "Can I have a nap while the bread bakes?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. Emmett covered his ears one more time. VROOM! The blender went again. "Ha!" said Emmett. "You can't be loud now."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Riley wanted to count the eggs for Grandma's cake. She found the basket on the quiet porch. Grandma said, "Ten eggs, please."

Riley counted out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" But only nine eggs sat on the table. One was missing!

"You skipped three, Riley," said Grandma with a smile. "Three comes after two. Try again, slow and steady."

Riley touched each egg as she said the words. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten eggs! The lost one had been hiding under a soft blanket.

"That's the one that got dry and cozy," Grandma teased.

Grandma cracked the eggs in the kitchen. Riley licked the spoon. "Best cake needs all ten," said Grandma.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: A swim teacher may hold a child while the child learns to float on their back.
story:
Leah was at the beach with her mom. They walked past the sand to a little pool. Leah wanted to float on her back. But she was scared. "What if I sink?" she asked. "I will be right here," said Miss Kim, the swim teacher.

Leah sat on the pool step. Her mom waved from a chair. Miss Kim held Leah's back with her hands. Leah leaned back into the water. She did not sink. The teacher's hands held her up. Leah looked at the sky. It was blue and wide. "I am floating!" she said. Miss Kim smiled. Her hands stayed under Leah's back. Leah kicked a little. Water splashed her chin.

After the swim, they went back to the sand. Mom had a crunchy snack and a small cake. Leah washed the sand off so she could bathe in the tub later. She closed her eyes and said, "Can we come back tomorrow?" Mom kissed her wet hair. "Yes, tomorrow we float again."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Birds are animals that have feathers.
story:
Hazel went out to the backyard with her teddy bear. She wanted to find something for a fairy picnic. She put down her toy truck and a red ball. Then she set out pretend food, a banana, crackers and a little cup of juice.

Under the big tree, she saw something soft. It was small and gray and light. "A feather!" said Hazel. "Birds are animals that have feathers. So a bird was here!" She held it up to her ear. It made no sound at all. It was quiet like a snowflake.

Then she heard a chirp. She looked up. A round little bird sat on the fence. It looked straight at the cracker in her hand. Hazel put the cracker on the grass. The bird flew down. It began to eat. Hazel whispered, "You can come to my fairy picnic too."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A flashlight with working batteries still shines when the power is out.
story:
The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules held his mama's hand. "Why is it so dark?" he asked. "The power is out," said Mama. "No power means no lights."

Jules felt a little scared. But Mama squeezed his hand. "We need the flashlight," she said. They patted the shelf. They patted the table. No flashlight. Then Jules thought of the kitchen. "The drawer!" he said. He planted his feet and walked slow, holding the wall. He felt the drawer handle. He pulled it open. His fingers found the flashlight inside.

"Will it work in the dark?" Jules asked. "Try it and see," said Mama. Jules pressed the button. A bright circle popped onto the wall. "It works!" he said. "The power is out, but the light is on!"

Mama lit a candle way up high, where Jules could not touch. Jules made his hand into a bunny shape in the flashlight beam. Two soft ears grew on the wall. Then something small glowed in the corner. It was his lost toy truck, shining in the light. It had been there all along. "You found my truck!" said Jules. He hugged the flashlight tight. "Dark house, bright light," he said. "That's true."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A square turned so a corner points up is still a square.
story:
Victor wanted to build a house for his toy bear. He looked for a square block. He found circles, which rolled away. He found triangles, which looked like little hats. He found a rectangle, long and flat. Where was the square?

Then Victor saw it. But it sat on a corner, all tilted. "That is a new shape," said his sister, Mia. Victor tipped it back down. It had four sides, all the same. It was his square! He stacked it under the rectangle roof.

Mia kissed the bear on its head. "Now bear has a home," she said.

"Next I will fly him to the moon," said Victor. He zoomed the bear round and round, over the square house and the triangle roof. "Zoom, zoom!" said Mia, and she flew her toy rabbit right beside him.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: The printed words in a book say the same thing every time the book is read.
story:
Aiden loves the dog book at school. It has a red dog on the front. Today he wants to hear it again.

Miss Pam sits down with the class. She opens the front of the book. She reads the first page. "Red Dog runs to the park." Aiden listens to every word.

After nap time, Mia's dad comes to read. He lifts the same red dog book. Aiden gets upset for a tiny moment. "That is not Miss Pam," he thinks. "Will the story be new words?"

But Mia's dad opens the front of the book. He reads the first page. "Red Dog runs to the park." The very same words! Aiden claps his hands.

Now Aiden has an idea. He takes the book to his teacher. "Your turn," he says. She smiles and turns to the first page.

"Red Dog runs to the park," she reads.

Aiden nods. "Same words," he says. "Every time."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby cannot talk yet, so it cries to show it needs something.
story:
Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was here! The baby was her little brother, Sam. His crib had a flat, soft blanket. Natalie patted it very gently.

Then Sam began to cry. Loud cries! Natalie put her hands over her ears. "Why is he crying?" she asked. She thought and thought. Maybe he wanted her teddy? She gave him the teddy. Sam kept crying. Maybe he wanted her sticker? She held it up high. Sam kept crying.

Mommy came in. "He is telling us something," Mommy said. "The baby cannot talk yet, so he cries to show he needs something." Mommy gave Sam warm milk. Sam drank and drank. Then the crying stopped! A big smile came on his face.

Natalie clapped her hands. "He talks with crying!" she said. Later, Sam cried again. Natalie ran fast down the hall like a little road. "Mommy! Sam is talking!" she called. Mommy picked Sam up, and Sam grabbed Natalie's finger and held on tight.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Holding your nose closed makes food taste less strong.
story:
Austin sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His mother sat next to him. He heard the door click. He saw a nurse with a small cup. The nurse smiled. "Time for your medicine," she said.

Austin did not want yucky medicine. He saw the pink cup. He smelled it. It smelled like strawberries. He touched the cup. It felt squishy on the sides. The nurse said, "You can pinch your nose closed, if you like."

Austin pinched his nose closed. Then he drank. He opened his eyes wide. The medicine tasted plain, not strong at all! He let go of his nose. He sniffed the air. The strawberry smell came back. He took one more sip with his nose open. That sip tasted strong again.

"Yum," said Austin. His mother laughed. The nurse gave him a sticker. It was a shiny star. Austin pressed it on his hand. Then he yawned a big yawn. He was ready to sleep on the ride home. His mother picked him up and held him close. "Strawberry next time," whispered the nurse.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Hunter wanted to bang his drum. But the baby was asleep.

Bang! Bang! Bang! The drum was loud. The baby woke up and cried.

Dad ran in. "Shh," he said. "Loud and quiet are opposites." He took the baby to rock her.

Hunter sat and thought. He tapped the drum. Tap. Tap. The drum was quiet now. The baby went back to sleep.

Hunter smiled. He tapped fast. Tap-tap-tap! Then he tapped slow. Tap... tap... tap.

Dad came back. "Nice and quiet," he whispered. He gave Hunter a thumbs up.

Outside, the sky looked stormy. Rain hit the window fast. But inside, Hunter's drum stayed soft.

Tap. Tap. The baby slept on.

Dad peeked in again. "My quiet drummer," he whispered. Hunter tapped one more little tap.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A square has four sides that are all the same length.
story:
Madelyn sat on the playroom rug. She wanted to build a house for her toy sheep. She had blocks of many shapes.

First she tried a triangle block. It wobbled and fell. "That will not fit," she said. Next she tried a circle block. It rolled away. The sheep looked sad in the weak little pile.

Then Madelyn found a square block. She took a piece of string. She laid it along one side. She laid it along the next side, and the next, and the next. All four sides were the same. "Four sides, all the same," she said. She stacked more squares. The wall stood tall and still.

She put on a triangle roof. She made a rectangle door. The sheep went inside. "Now your house will fit you," Madelyn said. The sheep sat down in its square house, safe and snug.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Saying how you feel, like "I feel sad," helps grown-ups know how to help you.
story:
Raphael built a big tower at school. It had ten blocks. Then Ben bumped the table. The tower fell down. All the blocks went crash.

Raphael felt angry. His face got hot. He sat in the corner and did not talk. Miss Kim came over. She knelt down by his chair.

"How do you feel?" she asked.

Raphael thought. Then he said, "I feel sad. My tower fell."

Miss Kim nodded. "I can help you build it again," she said.

Raphael felt excited. "A real big tower?" he asked.

"Yes, a real big one," said Miss Kim. "Maybe we can put a star block on top."

Raphael and Ben built a new tower together. The star block fit just right on top. Ben clapped. Raphael felt happy again.

"I like our tower," said Raphael. "Me too," said Ben.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
story:
Everett sat at the dinner table. He looked with his eyes at his carrots. Crunch, crunch, his ears heard the sound. Then the room went dark. The big light went out. "Oh no," said Everett. He could not see his carrots. He could not see his cup. He could not see his teddy bear, who sat in his chair.

Everett touched his plate with his hands. His fingers felt the rough edge. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled warm bread. He took a lick of his cup and his tongue tasted milk. But still, no teddy. "I want Teddy!" he said. He froze and waited.

"I will turn on the lamp," said Grandma. Click. The little lamp made a soft glow. Now Everett could see with his eyes again. There was Teddy, right on the chair. "Found you!" said Everett, and he gave Teddy a big hug.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'Can you help me, please?' is a way to ask for help when something is too hard.
story:
Lennon sat at the snack table. A jar of crackers sat in front of her. The lid would not come off. She pulled and pulled. Her hands slipped. The lid stayed stuck.

Maybe her teacher knew a trick. "Can you help me, please?" Lennon asked. Her teacher smiled. "Of course I can." She held the jar and turned the lid. Pop! The lid came off.

Lennon picked up a cracker and put it in her mouth. It was crunchy and good. Then she tipped her cup. Milk spilled on the table. "Oh no," she said. "Sorry about that." The teacher brought a towel. Lennon helped wipe it up.

At home time, her dad's phone buzzed in his pocket. She spotted her dad by the door. "Can you help me, please?" she asked again. "Help you with what?" he said. Lennon pointed at her spotted shoe. "My shoe is stuck on my foot." Her dad laughed and bent down. "One shoe, coming off." Pop! The shoe came free too.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: When someone says 'thank you', people often answer 'you're welcome.'
story: Cooper sat in the middle of the back seat. Mama was driving. Cooper wanted his water cup. It was far away on the floor. "Mama, can you help me, please?" he asked. Mama stopped at a red light. She reached back and gave him the cup. "Thank you," said Cooper. "You're welcome," said Mama. Cooper took a big sip. "Why do you say that?" he asked. Mama smiled. "You say it after thank you," she said. Cooper tried it in his head. One: thank you. Two: you're welcome. At the next stop, Cooper dropped his toy. It went under the seat. "Sorry, toy," he said. "Mama, please help me again." She reached back and got it. "Thank you, Mama." "You're welcome, Cooper." He laughed and hugged his toy. The car was quiet now. Cooper looked out the window. "Mama?" he said. "Yes, love?" "I like your words." Mama patted his shoe and drove home.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: A kitchen timer beeps or rings to tell the cook it is time to check the food.
story:
Gabriella put muffin mix in a bowl. She stirred it round and round. Dad poured the mix into little cups. Then the cups went into the big oven. Dad was the one who touched the hot oven door.

Dad turned a little round knob. It was an old timer, white and shiny. "Now we wait," said Dad. "How long?" asked Gabriella. "Until the timer beeps," said Dad. "The beep tells us it is time to check the muffins."

While they waited, the family played a game. They hid beans under cups. Gabriella watched the cups. She found the red bean twice! Mom laughed. Dad laughed too. Then everyone forgot about muffins. The game was so much fun.

Beep! Beep! Beep! The little timer rang out loud. "The muffins!" said Gabriella. Dad put on big mitts. He opened the oven door. Warm air came out. The muffins were big and gold. Gabriella sniffed the sweet smell. "The beep helped us remember," she said. She bit into a warm muffin. "Mmm," said Gabriella. "Like honey by the river."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A circle is round and has no corners.
story:
Rowan wanted to make cookies. Mom said, "Let's cut shapes in the dough." Rowan picked a square cutter. Press, press. The square cookie had four corners. He picked a triangle cutter. Press, press. The triangle cookie had three corners. Then Rowan picked the circle cutter. He looked for a corner to start on. He looked and looked. "Where is a corner?" he asked. Mom smiled. "A circle is round and has no corners," she said. Rowan touched the edge. It went round and round with no corners anywhere. "No corners!" he said. "No corners," said Mom again.

Rowan pressed the circle into the dough. Press, press. A round cookie sat on the tray. Then a big surprise. Rowan turned the circle cookie sideways. It still looked the same. The square cookie looked different when he turned it. The circle never did. He laughed out loud.

Mom put the tray in the oven. Rowan watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled sweet. Mom hummed a little song while they waited. Rowan hummed too. The cookies came out golden. Rowan found his circle cookie on the plate. He held it up to the window. The round sun was outside. "Look, Mom! The sun has no corners too!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. "Good looking, Rowan." Rowan took a big bite. The cookie was round all the way to the last crumb.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
story:
Cooper ran fast to the kitchen. He wanted cold milk for his playroom picnic. He pulled the fridge door open. Brrr! Cold air touched his toes. He could smell the apples inside. Cooper took the milk and ran back. He left the fridge door open.

Dad came in. "The door is open," he said. "Can you make it closed? Open and closed are opposites." Cooper pushed the door shut. Click! Now it was closed.

Back in the playroom, Cooper set up his picnic. His big teddy sat on the big chair. His small mouse sat on the small block. Cooper filled the toy teapot. "Tea is hot," said Dad, holding the cup far from Cooper's little fingers. Cooper touched his own cup instead. It was cold.

Cooper poured slowly, slowly. Then he stirred fast, fast, fast. He looked at the fridge across the room. Its door was closed. "Closed door," said Cooper, and gave teddy a drink.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you.
story: Isla stood in the bathroom. "Let's play hide and seek," said Mama. Isla wanted to hide in a good spot. She squeezed behind the towel rack. Then she covered her eyes with her hands. Now she could not see the tub. She could not see the sink. She could not see anything at all. Isla smiled. "Mama cannot see me," she thought. She heard the tap drip, drip, drip with her ears. She smelled the soap with her nose. Her tummy felt happy. "I see you, Isla!" said Mama. Isla peeked through her fingers. Mama was looking right at her! Isla took her hands away. Now she could see the mirror and the tidy shelf. "I saw your toes," said Mama, laughing. "Covering your eyes hides them from you, not from me." Isla laughed too. Then she licked her lips and tasted a bit of toothpaste, sweet and minty. She touched the soft towel with her fingers. "My turn to count," said Mama. She covered her eyes. "One, two, three," said Mama. Isla ran to hide. This time she left her eyes open wide.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Jasmine sat at the big table. She wanted to draw a sunny day. She picked up a gray crayon. She wanted the sky to be gray. Then she looked out the window. The sun was bright. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue. Jasmine put down the gray crayon. She picked up the blue crayon. She drew and drew. "Blue sky," she said.

Now she wanted a sun. She chose the yellow crayon. She made a big yellow circle. The yellow circle made the paper look warm. She looked out the window again. The yellow sun made the sky bright and blue. The blue crayon made her sun shine on the paper. One thing helped the other thing.

Jasmine drew green grass next. Then she drew red apples on a tree. "Mama, come see my party!" she called. Mama came to the table. "What a pretty day," said Mama. "I made it," said Jasmine. "The sky is blue today." Mama smiled at the blue crayon. Jasmine gave her a red apple to eat. "I'm hungry," said Mama. "Is it snack time?" Jasmine marched to the kitchen with her picture held high.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: If milk spills, you can wipe it up with a cloth.
story:
Colton stood in the restaurant kitchen. It was warm and noisy. A cook had made toast, and now the toast sat on a cool plate.

Colton wanted to help. Papa gave him a small knife with no sharp edge and some soft butter. Colton dipped the knife in the butter. He spread it on the toast. Slow, slow strokes. The butter made the toast shine.

Then Papa handed him a little cup of milk. Colton poured it into his big cup. Some milk ran over the edge. A little puddle sat on the table.

"What can I do?" Colton asked.

"You can wipe it up with a cloth," said Papa.

Colton took a cloth from the shelf. He wiped the puddle. The table was dry again. He picked up the cup and took a small, careful sip.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, walk slowly and hold a grown-up's hand so nobody trips.
story:
The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything was dark. Kai could not see his toy truck.

"I want my flashlight!" said Kai. He ran to the kitchen. Bump! His leg hit a chair. "Ow!" said Kai.

Dad came fast. Dad held Kai's hand. "In the dark, walk slowly," said Dad. "Hold my hand so nobody trips." Kai held on tight. They took one slow step. Then another slow step. Dad found the flashlight on the shelf and turned it on.

"Now we can have a dark party!" said Dad. They made shadows on the wall. A bunny! A big bird! Kai laughed. "This dark party is pretty fun," said Kai. Then the lights came back on. Kai clapped his hands. "We did it, Dad!"

"I want to do it again tomorrow," said Kai.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Rain boots keep your feet dry when you step in puddles.
story:
Julia woke up and looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. She put on her sun hat. Then she saw clouds come. The sky turned gray. It began to rain.

Julia wanted to jump in puddles. She ran to the door in her sneakers. Mama held her coat for her. "Rain boots," said Mama. Julia put on her yellow rain boots. One boot, two boots. She stomped outside.

The wind blew. It was a windy day too. Her hat flew off her head! Julia held her hat with both hands. She laughed and chased it around the yard.

Then Julia found a big puddle. She stepped right in. Splash! She looked at her boots. Her feet were dry. "My feet are dry," she said. She stepped in again. Splash! Still dry. Boots keep feet dry.

Later the rain stopped. Julia drew pictures inside. She drew a sunny sun, a rainy cloud, a windy tree, and white snow. "Snowy days need mittens," said Mama. Julia drew red mittens.

Mama cut toast into a triangle shape. Julia took a bite. "Tasty," she said. She held up her milk cup. "Toast, milk, boots," said Julia. "Dry feet all day." Then she stomped her boots on the floor, one, two, one, two.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book.
story:
Felix loved the big book about the sea. He loved the fish. He loved the whale. He wanted to know who drew the whale. "Miss Ana, who made this picture?" he asked. Miss Ana smiled. "The person who draws the pictures is called the illustrator," she said. Felix looked at the front of the book. There was a name there. "James Bell," he read, slow and careful. "That name is real writing," said Miss Ana. "The words tell us who did it."

Felix opened the book the right way. He started at the front. He turned one page. Then another page. The whale came last, so he had to wait. Waiting was hard, but Felix kept going. He turned pages one by one until the whale came.

At snack time, Felix had a pretzel. It was salty and crunchy. "I need to show Sam the whale," he said. He found Sam. Sam looked at the front of the book. "Who drew the fish?" Sam asked. Felix pointed at the name. "James Bell," he said. "He is the illustrator. Now you know a surprise too."

Sam turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the whale.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Things can be sorted into groups, like animals, toys and foods.
story:
Connor sat at the dinner table. He was very hungry. He wanted his pasta now.

"First, a game," said Mom. She put a big basket by his plate. It was full of little pictures.

Connor tipped the basket over. All the pictures fell out. There were dogs, cats, monkeys, apples, bananas, balls, blocks and more.

"Make three piles," said Dad. "Animals go together. Toys go together. Foods go together."

Connor picked up a monkey picture. He set it with the dog and the cat. Then he found a ball and a block. He patted that pile. "Toys!" he said.

He put apples and bananas in the last pile. His tummy growled loud.

"Good sorting," said Mom. "Now the foods pile helps you. Pasta is a food too."

She set down his warm bowl. Connor wore his biggest smile and picked up his fork.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Jordan runs to the block corner at daycare. Yesterday he built a big tower there. He wants to build it again today.

Jordan stacks one block. He stacks another block. The tower grows tall. Now it is as tall as his tummy.

His friend Milo walks over. "I went to the park tomorrow," says Milo. Milo stops and thinks. "No, not tomorrow. It already happened. I went yesterday."

Jordan looks at his tower. "Yesterday is before today," he says. He taps his blocks. "Yesterday my tower fell down. It went boom."

Jordan pushes the top block a tiny bit. The whole tower wobbles. Then it falls down. Boom! All the blocks are flat on the carpet.

"Again!" says Milo.

"Okay," says Jordan. "But first we clean up. Later we build more."

Miss Kim, the teacher, comes over. "What good builders you are," she says. "It is winter now, so we play inside. Tomorrow we will paint snowflakes."

Jordan stacks the blocks back in the box. He looks out the window. The sky is white and cold.

"Tomorrow," he says. "That is the next day."

"Let's build the tallest one," says Milo.

Jordan grabs a red block. "This one goes first."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Henry went to the park with Mom today. Yesterday it rained, so the swings were wet. Today the sun was out and warm.

Henry wanted to swing high. But a big boy was on the swing now. Henry had to wait. "When will it be my turn?" he asked. Mom pointed to the big clock by the gate. "The clock shows what time it is," she said. The long hand moved a little. Henry watched it. Then the big boy jumped off. "Now it is my turn!" said Henry.

He swung high, high, high. His sweater puffed out like a balloon. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Later we will go home and have a snack." Henry pumped his legs once more. The clock by the gate ticked on.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
story:
Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her father put down a plate of noodles. Zoey was excited. "Noodles are my favorite!" she said.

Then she saw her father's face. His eyes were wet. Tears ran down. Zoey felt scared. "Daddy, why is your face wet?" she asked. "I feel sad today," her father said. "When I feel sad, I cry." Zoey looked at her noodles. Then she had an idea. She ran to her room. She came back with her bunny. The bunny had one bumpy ear from too much love.

"Here, Daddy," she said. "Bunny makes me happy when I feel sad." Her father smiled a little. He held the bunny. Then he laughed. "Bunny tickles my chin," he said. Zoey laughed too. After dinner, they chased each other around the couch, bunny hopping along behind them.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green.
story:
Evelyn sat at the big art table. She was painting a lion. The lion had a round orange face and a long tail.

Now Evelyn wanted grass under the lion. She looked for green paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint. But no green paint anywhere.

"Miss Ana, I need green," said Evelyn. "We can mix two colors," said Miss Ana. "Try your blue and your yellow."

Evelyn put blue on her brush. She put it in a cup. Then she put yellow in too. She stirred with her brush. Round and round she stirred.

The paint turned green! Evelyn clapped her hands. "Look, look!" she said.

She painted green grass all under the lion. Tomás looked over from his seat. "I need green too," he said. "Here," said Evelyn. She showed him her blue cup and her yellow cup.

Tomás mixed his blue and yellow. His paint turned green too. He painted a big green tree.

Evelyn smiled at her lion in the green grass. "Blue and yellow," she said. "It worked!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
story:
Stella marched into daycare with a card in her hand. It was her birthday card from Grandma. On the front, Grandma had written Stella's name.

Stella put the card on the table. Then she looked at her cubby. Her name was there too. "Wait," said Stella. She looked at the card. She looked at the cubby. The letters were the same. S, then T, then the rest. Same letters, same order, both times.

"Sam, come look!" said Stella. Sam came over. He could see his name on his cubby. But he did not have a card. Stella got a pencil. "I will write your name," she said. She copied the letters from Sam's cubby. S, A, M. She wrote them on paper. Sam held the paper next to his cubby. The letters matched.

The room was noisy with kids playing. But Stella sat very still. She turned to the first page of her card and read the pictures front to back. Then she read them again. At the last page she said, "Grandma wrote my name. It looks just like my name on my cubby."

She put the card in her cubby, right under the letters.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
story:
Layla was building a tower in her room. The blocks were red and blue and yellow. She had an idea to make it very, very tall.

The sky got dark outside. Layla put on her pajamas. Then she heard a noise. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Layla felt scared. Her tummy felt small and tight.

She did not hide under the bed. She walked to the hall. "Mama, I hear a noise. I am scared," she said. Mama took her hand. "Let's go look together," said Mama. They went slowly. Tap, tap, tap. Mama opened the curtain. A small branch was touching the glass. The wind moved it. The wind made the branch tap.

"Wind," said Layla. She felt happy now. Mama tucked her into bed. The tap, tap, tap sounded different now. It sounded like a little song.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, your eyes slowly get used to it, and you can see more after a little while.
story:
The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules could not even see his own hands. "Where did my toys go?" he asked. Dad lit a little candle and said, "Let's sit on the back step while we wait." So they did.

The backyard was very dark at first. Jules saw nothing. He sat still and counted the stars. One, two, three, four. "Is that snow in the sky?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "Those are stars." He counted some more. Then something funny happened. He could see the big tree. Then he could see his red ball. Then he could see his toy fish lying in the grass.

"Is it a real fish?" he asked. "No," said Dad. "It is a toy." Jules laughed. His eyes waited in the dark, and now they could see so much. He patted the tree, then the ball, then the fish. "Hello, dark," he said. "Hello, Jules," said Mom, in her best dark voice.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: A lost and found is a place where people put things they find, so the owners can get them back.
story:
Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there.

"Bunny is lost," said Aubrey. She looked under the blanket. She looked in her cup drawer. No bunny.

Grandma came in. "Let's look together," she said. They looked by the big chair. They looked by the door.

Then Grandma opened a small basket. "This is our lost and found," she said. "We put things we find in here. Then people can get them back."

Aubrey peeked in. There was a hairbrush. There was one glove. There was a shiny spoon.

And there, at the bottom, was bunny!

"Found you!" said Aubrey. She hugged bunny tight.

Then she saw something else. A little red sock sat in the basket. "Grandpa's sock?" asked Aubrey.

Grandpa popped his head in. "My sock! I lost it last week," he said.

Aubrey held it up. "You can get it back," she said. Grandpa laughed and put the sock on his foot.

Then Aubrey shared her cereal with bunny. She gave bunny a bite from her spoon. Bunny liked breakfast, too.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Many pools have a shallow end and a deep end.
story:
Victoria went to the beach with her mom. The beach had a big pool next to the sand. Victoria wanted to swim there. Her big sister Rosa swam far out in the sea. Victoria wanted to swim far too.

The swim teacher named Miss Kim said, "We start at the shallow end." Victoria stood in the water there. The water came up to her tummy. She could touch the bottom. Rosa stood far away. The water went up to Rosa's shoulders. "That part is the deep end," Rosa called.

Miss Kim held Victoria's hands. Victoria kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. The wind pushed little waves near her cheek. They waited, then she kicked again. She found a slimy leaf in the water and dropped it in the sand.

Victoria walked back to the shallow end. She kicked some more. Her feet lifted up, up, up. "Look, Mom! I'm swimming!" she said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had red paint and blue paint. He wanted to paint a big flower for his mom. He was wearing his favorite blue shirt.

Mama came in with a bowl of water. "Let's put on your old shirt first," she said. She pulled a big green shirt over his head. It went down past his elbows.

Mohamed dipped his brush. He made red dots and blue dots. He made a tall green stem. Then a big blue splat went right on his shirt. But it landed on the green shirt, not the blue one. "The paint did not get on me," said Mohamed. He made another dot. That one splashed too. The green shirt caught that one as well.

Mama held up the painting. The flower had a red middle and blue petals. "I will hang it up," she said. Mohamed looked at his arms. Under the green shirt, his favorite blue shirt was still clean. He smiled and pointed at it. "Look, Mama. Still clean."
